thread.title: Tree Assistance Program expanded as growers face 2026 fire blight outbreak
thread.title_full: Tree Assistance Program expanded as growers face 2026 fire blight outbreak

author: Keystone Today
title: Tree Assistance Program expanded as growers face 2026 fire blight outbreak
text:
The Tree Assistance Program, reauthorized under the 2018 Farm Bill and proposed for expansion in the 2026 Farm Bill, provides financial assistance to orchardists and nursery tree growers who need to replant or rehabilitate trees, bushes, and vines damaged by natural disasters, according to a May 27 announcement. The program covers commercial plantings such as fruit, nut, ornamental, and Christmas trees. Recent losses due to wet weather, winter injury, insect damage, and disease have made TAP a potential resource for affected growers.
To qualify for TAP assistance, fruit growers and nurserymen must show tree losses exceeding 15 percent of their stand (adjusted for normal mortality) resulting from an eligible natural disaster. Losses must not have been preventable through reasonable management practices and must be visible or otherwise substantiated to the USDA-Farm Service Agency inspector. For plant diseases or insect infestations where loss is not visible, evidence from a qualified expert may be required.
Eligible producers approved for compensation under TAP are required to replace affected plants within 12 months of application approval. Payments begin when mortality exceeds the threshold: TAP covers up to 65 percent of actual replanting costs or 50 percent of rehabilitation costs. Eligibility also requires an average Adjusted Gross Income below $900,000 per individual or entity. Changes introduced by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 removed payment limitations per person or legal entity and increased the acreage cap per year.
The deadline for submitting a TAP claim is either within 60 days after a declared disaster event or within 90 days of when the loss becomes apparent. For more information on filing claims or details about eligibility requirements, producers are advised to contact their local USDA-FSA office.
In response to severe fire blight conditions during the recent bloom season in orchards across Pennsylvania in 2026, Penn State Extension recommends continued scouting for fire blight infections. Prohexadione calcium (ProCa; Kudos or Apogee) is recommended at high label rates to slow infection spread by hardening off shoots over ten to fourteen days following application. Additionally, FungOUT—a citric acid-based product—was evaluated this year at Penn State FREC as a possible option against active fire blight infections; however, its effectiveness remains unproven since this is its first trial year.
Penn State Extension advises prioritizing pruning efforts using a triage method based on orchard age and severity of infection while avoiding excessive cutting that could worsen outbreaks through new shoot growth. Recommendations include removing infected tissue early before necrosis develops; focusing on young high-density plantings if incidence is high; practicing methods like ugly stub cuts; disposing prunings appropriately; and considering “Actigard Paint” treatment after pruning cuts but avoiding leaf exposure due to phytotoxicity risk.
Penn State Extension delivers science-based education throughout Pennsylvania via local offices and digital tools with programming focused on agriculture—including pest control—and collaborates with government agencies as well as industry partners, according to Penn State Extension .
